<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><A NAME="toc488260_3"></A>Item&#8201;1. Business. </B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>The
Fund </B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We were formed on March&nbsp;20, 2026, as a Delaware statutory trust and converted to a Maryland corporation effective on
September 18, 2026. We were organized to invest primarily in a portfolio of newly originated, privately negotiated first-lien senior secured loans to U.S. middle market companies. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We operate as an externally managed, <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-diversified,</FONT>
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">closed-end</FONT> management investment company that intends to file an election to be regulated as a BDC under the 1940 Act (the date of our filing of our election to be regulated as a BDC under the 1940 Act is
referred to in this Registration Statement as the &#8220;<U>BDC Election Date</U>&#8221;). In addition, following the BDC Election Date, we intend to, as soon as reasonably practicable, qualify and elect to be treated for federal income tax
purposes, and intend to qualify annually thereafter, as a RIC under the Code. Prior to its qualification as a RIC, the Fund will be taxed as a C-corporation for U.S. federal income tax purposes. See &#8220;<I>Item&nbsp;1. Business &#8212; Regulation
as a Business Development Company</I>&#8221; and &#8220;<I>Item 1. Business &#8212; Certain U.S. Federal Income Tax Considerations.</I>&#8221; We commenced investment operations concurrent with the closing of the SPV Contribution (as defined below).
See &#8220;<I>Item 1. Business &#8212; Seed Investment and Initial Portfolio.</I>&#8221; </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We intend to operate as a <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-exchange</FONT> traded, perpetual-life BDC, which is a BDC whose common shares are not listed for trading on a stock exchange or other securities market. We use the term &#8220;perpetual-life BDC&#8221; to describe an
investment vehicle of indefinite duration, whose common shares are intended to be sold by the BDC on a continuous monthly basis at a price equal to the BDC&#8217;s then-current monthly net asset value (&#8220;<U>NAV</U>&#8221;) per share. In our
perpetual-life structure, we may offer investors an opportunity to have their shares repurchased on a quarterly basis at NAV, but we are not obligated to offer to repurchase any shares in any particular quarter in our discretion. We believe that our
perpetual nature will enable us to execute a patient and opportunistic strategy and </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">6 </P>

</DIV></Center>


<p style="margin-top:1em; margin-bottom:0em; page-break-before:always"> </p>

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">
be able to invest across different market environments. This may reduce the risk of the Fund being a forced seller of assets in market downturns compared to
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-perpetual</FONT> funds. While we may consider a liquidity event at any time in the future, we currently do not intend to undertake a liquidity event, and we are not obligated by our articles of incorporation (as
amended, restated, supplemented or otherwise modified from time to time, the &#8220;<U>charter</U>&#8221;), or our bylaws (collectively, with our charter, as each may be amended, restated, supplemented or otherwise modified from time to time, the
&#8220;<U>Organizational Documents</U>&#8221;) or otherwise to effect a liquidity event at any time. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Our Board of Directors (the
&#8220;<U>Board</U>&#8221; or the &#8220;<U>Board of Directors</U>&#8221;) may, in its sole discretion, determine to cause the Fund to conduct a &#8220;<U>Liquidity Event</U>,&#8221; which is defined as including (1)&nbsp;an initial public offering
(&#8220;<U>IPO</U>&#8221;) or other listing of the Common Shares on a national securities exchange (an &#8220;<U>Exchange Listing</U>&#8221;), or (2)&nbsp;a Sale Transaction. A &#8220;<U>Sale Transaction</U>&#8221; means (a)&nbsp;the sale of all or
substantially all of the Fund&#8217;s assets to, or other liquidity event with, another entity or (b)&nbsp;a transaction or series of transactions, including by way of merger, consolidation, recapitalization, reorganization, or sale of stock in each
case for consideration of either cash and/or publicly listed securities of the acquirer. A Sale Transaction also may include a sale, merger or other transaction with one or more affiliated investment companies managed by the Adviser or an affiliate
thereof. The decision to cause the Fund to conduct a Liquidity Event will take into consideration factors such as prevailing market conditions at the time and the Fund&#8217;s portfolio composition. The ability of the Fund to commence and consummate
a Liquidity Event is not assured, and will depend on a variety of factors, including the size and composition of the Fund&#8217;s portfolio and prevailing market conditions at the time. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Until such time as the Board determines to cause the Fund to conduct a Liquidity Event, the Fund will remain a privately offered BDC and, in
its commercially reasonable judgment, expects to conduct quarterly repurchases of its Common Shares. See &#8220;<I>Item 1. Business &#8212; Discretionary Share Repurchase Program.</I>&#8221; </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Our primary investment objective is to generate current income, while maintaining downside protection. We seek to pursue our investment
objective by investing primarily in a portfolio of newly originated, privately negotiated first-lien senior secured loans to U.S. middle market companies. We generally use the term &#8220;middle market&#8221; to refer to companies with between
$5&nbsp;million to $100&nbsp;million in annual earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (&#8220;<U>EBITDA</U>&#8221;). Although we expect to invest primarily in middle market companies with between $10&nbsp;million to
$75&nbsp;million in annual EBITDA, we may invest, to a lesser extent, in companies with higher (or lower) EBITDA. In addition, we seek to pursue our investment objective by: </P> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">
<TR style = "page-break-inside:avoid">
<TD WIDTH="5%">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="3%" VALIGN="top" ALIGN="left">&#149;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="1%" VALIGN="top">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">utilizing the experience and expertise of the management team of the Adviser; </P></TD></TR></TABLE>
<P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">

<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">maintaining rigorous portfolio monitoring in an attempt to anticipate and
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">pre-empt</FONT> negative credit events within our portfolio, such as an event of insolvency, liquidation, dissolution, reorganization or bankruptcy of a portfolio company. </P></TD></TR></TABLE>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Though no assurance can be given that the Fund will achieve its investment objective, we believe that a disciplined, credit-driven approach
focused on seniority in the capital structure, collateral support and lender-oriented documentation can help mitigate downside risk across market environments. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We expect to allocate primarily to three types of assets: (a)&nbsp;direct private credit investments originated by us, including <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">co-investments</FONT> with other Sagard credit strategies, relationships with banks, healthcare and royalty lending, and other private credit opportunities; (b)&nbsp;asset-based opportunities, such as whole loans,
collateralized loan obligations (&#8220;<U>CLOs</U>&#8221;) and equity investments, including funds and/or pooled investment vehicles managed by us or one or more third-party managers, that have the potential to generate attractive yields with
downside </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">7 </P>

protection; and (c)&nbsp;broadly syndicated loans (&#8220;<U>BSLs</U>&#8221;), which are expected to provide a degree of liquidity within the portfolio. We generally expect our investments to be
floating-rate instruments and to generate returns primarily through contractual interest payments and, where applicable, original issue discounts and customary fees associated with privately negotiated lending transactions. From time to time, we may
also pursue asset-based opportunities consistent with our focus on capital preservation.</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In addition, we expect to focus primarily on <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-sponsored</FONT> borrowers and may also invest in sponsor-backed companies, to a lesser extent. Investment sizes in corporate borrowers will vary based on, among other things, our capital availability, the composition
of our portfolio, and general micro- and macro-economic factors. As discussed below, while we will primarily seek to make private credit investments in senior, first-lien secured loans in U.S. middle market companies, we may also invest
opportunistically in &#8220;event-driven&#8221; and other special situations, and, to a lesser extent, secondary purchases of debt investments and other dislocated or distressed credit opportunities, where the Adviser believes such investments are
consistent with our investment objective and capital preservation focus. Any opportunistic investments will be subject to the same disciplined underwriting standards described in this Registration Statement, adjusted as appropriate to reflect the
nature of the applicable opportunity. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We, through the Adviser, expect to source opportunities through a multi-channel origination
approach and to apply a disciplined underwriting process designed to evaluate business fundamentals, cash flow durability, leverage and liquidity, collateral and documentation terms and downside scenarios. Following investment, we expect to actively
monitor portfolio investments with a focus on the early identification of issues and proactive risk management consistent with our capital preservation focus. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">See &#8220;<I>Item 1. Business &#8212; Investment Objectives and Strategy</I>&#8221; below for more information. </P>

jurisdictions where any offering is made to investors who are &#8220;accredited investors&#8221; within the meaning of Rule&nbsp;501(a) of Regulation D promulgated under the Securities Act. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Seed Investment and Initial Portfolio </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Seed Investment </I></B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">On
September 30, 2026, prior to the BDC Election Date, SHI made the $25,000 Seed Investment in the Fund in exchange for 2,500 Class&nbsp;I shares. The proceeds of the Seed Investment were used for general organization and operational purposes of the
Fund. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>SPV Contribution and Initial Portfolio </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Fund commenced investment operations in connection with the closing of a contribution transaction on October 27, 2026 (the &#8220;<U>SPV
Contribution</U>&#8221;), after which the Fund expects to file its election to be regulated as a BDC under the 1940&nbsp;Act. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In
connection with the SPV Contribution, the Fund acquired all of the limited partnership interests of Sagard Private Income Fund SPV I LP (&#8220;<U>SPV I</U>&#8221;), a special purpose vehicle formed as a Delaware limited partnership in May 2026,
which holds a portfolio of U.S. dollar-denominated, first-lien senior secured direct lending investments and which comprises the Fund&#8217;s initial investment portfolio (the &#8220;<U>Initial Portfolio</U>&#8221;). In connection with the SPV
Contribution, the Fund also acquired all of the equity interests in SPV I&#8217;s general partner. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Initial Portfolio has been
originated and managed by investment personnel of the Adviser and consists of investments consistent with the Fund&#8217;s investment objective and strategy, including the qualifying asset requirements applicable to BDCs under the 1940 Act and the
asset diversification requirements applicable to RICs under the Code. The aggregate purchase price for the limited partnership interests of SPV I in the SPV Contribution was approximately $76.5&nbsp;million, which is equal to the NAV of SPV I as of
closing of the SPV Contribution. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The valuation of the Initial Portfolio at the time of the closing of the SPV Contribution was based on
the fair values of each asset and unfunded commitment in the Initial Portfolio as of the date of the SPV Contribution, as determined in accordance with the Adviser&#8217;s valuation policies and procedures and in consultation with an independent
third-party valuation firm engaged by the Adviser. For purposes of determining the fair value of the Initial Portfolio, the assets and unfunded commitments in the Initial Portfolio were valued as of October 22, 2026 by an independent third-party
valuation firm. In connection with the closing of the SPV Contribution and the acquisition of the Initial Portfolio, the Adviser conducted certain valuation procedures to confirm whether there had been any material changes to the fair values of the
investments and obligations in the Initial Portfolio since </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">12 </P>

<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In exchange for the SPV Contribution, SHI&#8217;s wholly-owned subsidiary, Sagard Holdings Investment I LP, received&nbsp;7,654,277.44 Class I
shares, which amount equaled the net asset value of SPV I divided by the then-current NAV per Common Share, as determined in accordance with the Fund&#8217;s valuation policies and procedures. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Atlas Credit Facility </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In connection with the acquisition of the Initial Portfolio, SPV I entered into a revolving credit and security agreement (the &#8220;<U>Atlas
Credit Facility</U>&#8221;) by and among SPV I, the Adviser, as servicer, Atlas Securitized Products Administration, L.P., as administrative agent (&#8220;<U>Atlas</U>&#8221;), Atlas Securitized Products, L.P., as lead arranger, U.S. Bank Trust
Company, National Association, as collateral agent and collateral administrator, U.S. Bank National Association, as custodian and as document custodian, each of the managing agents from time to time party thereto and each of the conduit lenders and
institutional lenders from time to time party thereto.</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Atlas Credit Facility provides for $100&nbsp;million of initial commitments,
with an uncommitted accordion feature that allows for commitments up to $250&nbsp;million from new and existing lenders on the same terms as the existing commitments, subject to market conditions. U.S.&nbsp;Dollar advances under the Atlas Credit
Facility bear interest at three-month Term SOFR plus an applicable margin of 2.20% during the revolving period.&nbsp;Subject to certain performance conditions, the applicable margin could increase to 2.45% during the revolving period and could range
up to 2.55% during the amortization or End of Life Option periods.&nbsp;The Atlas Credit Facility provides for an unused commitment fee of, from the effective date through March&nbsp;17, 2027, 0.50% per annum on the Atlas Credit Facility&#8217;s
unused commitments up to the then-current committed facility amount and thereafter 0.50% per annum on the unused commitments up to 35% of the then-current committed facility amount and 0.75% per annum on the unused commitments in excess of 35% of
the then-current committed facility amount, together with a commitment reduction fee and other customary fees.&nbsp;The Atlas Credit Facility matures on June&nbsp;1, 2031, provided that SPV I and Atlas may mutually agree to extend the maturity date
to June&nbsp;1, 2033 pursuant to the &#8220;End of Life Option&#8221; under the Atlas Credit Facility.</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Atlas Credit Facility contains
customary terms and conditions, including affirmative and negative covenants. The credit agreement governing the Atlas Credit Facility also contains customary events of default including, without limitation, nonpayment, misrepresentation of
representations and warranties in a material respect and breach of covenant, bankruptcy and change of control, with customary cure and notice provisions. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">SPV I&#8217;s obligations to the lenders are secured by a first-priority perfected security interest in all of its assets and a pledge of the
equity interests in SPV I by its general partner and, following the SPV Contribution, the Fund, but are otherwise <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-recourse</FONT> to its general partner and the Fund.&#8195; </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In connection with the closing of the SPV Contribution, the Fund, as seller, and SPV I, as purchaser, will enter into a Purchase and
Contribution Agreement, pursuant to which the Fund may from time to time sell and contribute loans and related assets to SPV I at fair value. Under that agreement, the Fund will have certain indemnification obligations and may be required to
repurchase or substitute loans that fail to satisfy specified eligibility requirements when transferred, subject to applicable cure rights and exceptions.</P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Atlas and the lenders under the Atlas Credit Facility, and their respective affiliates, may from time to time receive customary fees and
expenses in the performance of investment banking, financial advisory or other services for the Fund. </P>

<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Discretionary Share Repurchase Program </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We do not intend to list our Common Shares on any securities exchange. Because no public market exists or is expected to exist for the Common
Shares, shareholders will likely have limited ability to sell their shares absent a liquidity event. We currently do not intend to undertake a liquidity event, other than the liquidity from the discretionary share repurchase program described below,
and we are not obligated by our Organizational Documents or otherwise to effect a liquidity event at any time. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Beginning no later than
the quarter ending June&nbsp;30, 2027, we intend to commence a share repurchase program pursuant to which we intend, subject to market conditions and the discretion of our Board, to offer to repurchase in each quarter, up to 5% of our Common Shares
outstanding as of the close of the previous calendar quarter. For the avoidance of doubt, such target amount is assessed each calendar quarter. Our Board may amend, suspend or terminate the share repurchase program at any time if it deems such
action to be in the best interest of our common shareholders, such as when a repurchase offer would place an undue burden on our liquidity, adversely affect our operations or risk having an adverse impact on the Fund that would outweigh the benefit
of the repurchase offer. As a result, share repurchases may not be available each quarter, or may only be available in an amount less than 5% of our Common Shares outstanding. We intend to conduct any such repurchase offers in accordance with the
requirements of Rule <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">13e-4</FONT> promulgated under the Exchange Act and the 1940 Act, with the terms of such tender offer published in a tender offer statement to be sent to all shareholders and filed with the SEC
on Schedule&nbsp;TO. To the extent we offer to repurchase Common Shares in any particular quarter, we expect to repurchase shares pursuant to tender offers using a purchase price equal to the NAV per share as of the last calendar day of a&nbsp;month
designated by our Board of Directors during the applicable quarter (the &#8220;<U>Valuation Date</U>&#8221;), which will not be available until after the expiration of the applicable tender offer. As a result, shareholders will not know the exact
repurchase price of shares in the tender offer when they make their decision whether to tender their Common Shares. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">If shareholders
tender Common Shares in a tender offer with a Valuation Date that is within the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">12-month</FONT> period following the initial issue date of their tendered Common Shares, the Fund may repurchase such Common Shares
subject to an &#8220;early repurchase deduction&#8221; of 2% of the aggregate NAV of the Common Shares repurchased (an &#8220;<U>Early</U> </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">16 </P>

qualifying disability (as such term is defined in Section&nbsp;72(m)(7) of the Code) or divorce of a shareholder who is a natural person, including Common Shares held by such shareholder through a trust or an individual retirement account or other
retirement or profit-sharing plan, after (i)&nbsp;in the case of death, receiving written notice from the estate of the shareholder, the recipient of the Common Shares through bequest or inheritance, or, in the case of a trust, the trustee of such
trust, who shall have the sole ability to request repurchase on behalf of the trust, (ii)&nbsp;in the case of qualified disability, receiving written notice from such shareholder, provided that the condition causing the qualifying disability was not
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">pre-existing</FONT> on the date that the shareholder became a shareholder of the Fund or (iii)&nbsp;in the case of divorce, receiving written notice from the shareholder of the divorce and the shareholder&#8217;s
instructions to effect a transfer of the Common Shares (through the repurchase of the Common Shares by us and the subsequent purchase by the shareholder) to a different account held by the shareholder (including a trust or an individual retirement
account or other retirement or profit-sharing plan). We must receive the written repurchase request within 12 months after the death of the shareholder, the initial determination of the shareholder&#8217;s disability or divorce in order for the
requesting party to rely on any of the special treatment described above that may be afforded in the event of the death, disability or divorce of a shareholder. In the case of death, such a written request must be accompanied by a certified copy of
the official death certificate of the shareholder. If spouses are joint registered holders of Common Shares, the request to have the Common Shares repurchased may be made if either of the registered holders dies or acquires a qualified disability.
If the shareholder is not a natural person, such as certain trusts or a partnership, corporation or other similar entity, the right to waiver of the Early Repurchase Deduction upon death, disability or divorce does not apply. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">You may tender all of the Common Shares that you own in connection with our discretionary quarterly tender offers. If shareholders seek to
have an amount of shares repurchased that exceeds the repurchase offer amount, shares will generally be repurchased on a pro rata basis; however, our Board may instead, in its sole discretion, choose to amend the repurchase offer and accept for
purchase all of our shares that were validly tendered. All unsatisfied repurchase requests do not carry over automatically and must be resubmitted in the next quarterly tender offer, or upon the recommencement of the discretionary share repurchase
program, as applicable. We will have no obligation to repurchase shares, including if the repurchase would violate the restrictions on distributions under federal law or Maryland law. The limitations and restrictions described above may prevent us
from accommodating all repurchase requests made in any quarter. Our discretionary share repurchase program has many limitations, including the limitations described above, and should not in any way be viewed as the equivalent of a secondary market.

 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We will offer to repurchase shares on such terms as may be determined by our Board in its
complete and absolute discretion unless, in the judgment of our Board, such repurchases would not be in the best interests of our shareholders or would violate applicable law. There is no assurance that the Board will exercise its discretion to
offer to repurchase shares or that there will be sufficient funds available to accommodate all of our common shareholders&#8217; requests for repurchase. As a result, we may repurchase less than the full amount of shares that you request to have
repurchased. If we do not repurchase the full amount of your shares that you have requested to be repurchased, or we determine not to make repurchases of our shares, you will likely not be able to dispose of your shares, even if we under-perform.
Any periodic repurchase offers will be subject in part to our available cash and compliance with the RIC qualification and diversification rules and the 1940 Act. Other than with respect to the Early Repurchase Deduction described above,
shareholders will not pay a fee to us in connection with our repurchase of Common Shares under the discretionary share repurchase program. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Fund will repurchase Common Shares from shareholders pursuant to written tenders on terms and conditions that the Board determines to be
fair to the Fund and to all shareholders. When the Board determines that the Fund will repurchase shares, notice will be provided to shareholders describing the terms of that particular offer, containing information shareholders should consider in
deciding whether to participate in the repurchase opportunity and containing information on how to participate. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Repurchases will be
effective after receipt and acceptance by the Fund of eligible written tenders of shares from shareholders by the applicable repurchase offer deadline. All shares purchased by us pursuant to the terms of each tender offer will be redeemed and
thereafter will be authorized and unissued shares. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The majority of our assets will consist of directly originated loans and other
instruments that generally cannot be readily liquidated without impacting our ability to realize their full value upon disposition. Therefore, we may not always have sufficient liquid resources to make repurchase offers. In order to provide
liquidity for share repurchases, we intend to generally maintain under normal circumstances a smaller allocation to broadly syndicated loans and other more liquid credit investments. We may fund repurchase requests from sources other than cash flow
from operations, including, without limitation, the sale of assets, borrowings, return of capital or offering proceeds, and although we generally expect to fund distributions from cash flow from operations we have not established any internal
policies or limits on the amounts we may pay from such sources. Should making repurchase offers, in our judgment, place an undue burden on our liquidity, adversely affect our operations or risk having an adverse impact on the company as a whole, or
should we otherwise determine that investing our liquid assets in self-originated loans or other illiquid investments rather than repurchasing our Common Shares is in the best interests of the Fund and our common shareholders as a whole, then we may
choose to offer to repurchase fewer shares than described above, or none at all. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In the event that any common shareholder fails to
maintain the minimum balance of $500 of our Common Shares, we may repurchase all of the shares held by that shareholder at the repurchase price in effect on the date we determine that the shareholder has failed to meet the minimum balance, less any
Early Repurchase Deduction. In the alternative, the Fund reserves the right to reduce the number of Common Shares requested to be repurchased from a shareholder so that the required account balance is maintained. Minimum account repurchases will
apply even in the event that the failure to meet the minimum balance is caused solely by a decline in our NAV. Minimum account repurchases are generally subject to an Early Repurchase Deduction, subject to the Fund&#8217;s right to waive such
deduction in its discretion in accordance with the waiver provisions described above. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Payment for repurchased shares may require us to
liquidate portfolio holdings earlier than our Adviser would otherwise have caused these holdings to be liquidated, potentially resulting in losses, and may increase our investment-related expenses as a result of higher portfolio turnover rates. Our
Adviser intends to take measures, subject to policies as may be established by our Board, to attempt to avoid or minimize potential losses and expenses resulting from the repurchase of shares. </P>

 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Investment Objectives and Strategy </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Overview </I></B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The
Fund&#8217;s primary investment objective is to generate current income, while maintaining downside protection. The Fund seeks to pursue this objective by investing primarily in a portfolio of newly originated, privately negotiated first-lien senior
secured loans to U.S. middle market companies. We generally use the term &#8220;middle market&#8221; to refer to companies with between $5&nbsp;million to $100&nbsp;million in annual EBITDA. Although the Fund expects to invest primarily in middle
market companies with between $10&nbsp;million to $75&nbsp;million in annual EBITDA, the Fund may invest, to a lesser extent, in companies with higher (or lower) EBITDA. Though no assurance can be given that the Fund will achieve its investment
objective, the Fund believes that a disciplined, credit-driven approach focused on seniority in the capital structure, collateral support and lender-oriented documentation can help mitigate downside risk across market environments.</P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Fund expects to allocate primarily to three types of assets: (a)&nbsp;direct private credit investments originated by us, including <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">co-investments</FONT> with other Sagard credit strategies, relationships with banks, healthcare and royalty lending, and other private credit opportunities; (b)&nbsp;asset-based opportunities, such as whole loans, CLOs and
equity investments, including funds and/or pooled investment vehicles managed by us or one or more third-party managers, that have the potential to generate attractive yields with downside protection; and (c)&nbsp;BSLs, which are expected to provide
a degree of liquidity within the portfolio. Under normal circumstances the Fund expects that the majority of its portfolio will be in privately originated and privately negotiated investments, predominantly direct lending to U.S. private companies
through (i)&nbsp;first lien senior secured and unitranche loans (including <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">first-out/last-out</FONT></FONT> loans) and, to a lesser extent, (ii)&nbsp;second lien, unsecured,
subordinated or mezzanine loans and structured credit, as well as BSLs (for which the Fund may serve as an anchor investor), club deals (generally investments made by a small group of investment firms) and other debt and equity securities. In
limited instances we may retain the &#8220;last out&#8221; portion of a first-lien loan. In such cases, the &#8220;first out&#8221; portion of the first lien loan would receive priority with respect to payment over our &#8220;last out&#8221;
position. In exchange for the higher risk of loss associated with such &#8220;last out&#8221; portion, we would earn a higher rate of interest than the &#8220;first out&#8221; position. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Fund generally expects its investments to be floating-rate instruments and to generate returns primarily through contractual interest
payments and, where applicable, original issue discounts and customary fees associated with privately negotiated lending transactions. From time to time, the Fund may also pursue asset-based opportunities consistent with its focus on capital
preservation.</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In addition, the Fund expects to focus primarily on <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-sponsored</FONT> borrowers and may
also invest in sponsor-backed companies, to a lesser extent. Investment sizes in corporate borrowers will vary based on, among other things, the Fund&#8217;s capital availability, the composition of the Fund&#8217;s portfolio, and general micro- and
macro-economic factors. As discussed below, while the Fund will primarily seek to make private credit investments in senior, first-lien secured loans in U.S. middle market companies, the Fund may also invest opportunistically in
&#8220;event-driven&#8221; and other special situations, and, to a lesser extent, secondary purchases of debt investments and other dislocated or distressed credit opportunities, where the Adviser believes such investments are consistent with the
Fund&#8217;s investment objective and capital preservation focus. Any opportunistic investments will be subject to the same disciplined underwriting standards described in this Registration Statement, adjusted as appropriate to reflect the nature of
the applicable opportunity. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Fund, through the Adviser, expects to source opportunities through a multi-channel origination approach
and to apply a disciplined underwriting process designed to evaluate business fundamentals, cash flow durability, leverage and liquidity, collateral and documentation terms and downside scenarios. Following investment, the Fund expects to actively
monitor portfolio investments with a focus on the early identification of issues and proactive risk management consistent with the Fund&#8217;s capital preservation focus. The Fund&#8217;s origination and monitoring processes are described in
greater detail under &#8220;<I>Investment Process</I>&#8221; below. </P>

calendar quarter after the BDC Election Date. Any distributions the Fund makes will be at the discretion of the Board, considering factors such as earnings, cash flow, capital needs and general financial condition and the requirements of Maryland

<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The instruments in which the Fund intends to invest typically will not be rated by any rating agency, but the Fund believes that in some cases,
if such instruments were rated, they would be below investment grade (rated lower than &#8220;Baa3&#8221; by Moody&#8217;s Investors Service, lower than <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;BBB-&#8221;</FONT> by Fitch Ratings or lower than <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;BBB-&#8221;</FONT> by Standard&nbsp;&amp; Poor&#8217;s Ratings Services), which, under the guidelines established by these entities, is an indication of having predominantly speculative characteristics with respect
to the issuer&#8217;s capacity to pay interest and repay principal. Debt that is rated below investment grade is sometimes referred to as &#8220;high yield&#8221; or &#8220;junk&#8221; debt. The Fund may invest without limit in debt or other
securities of any rating, as well as unrated debt or other securities. The Fund&#8217;s approach to credit risk management focuses on fundamental underwriting, structural protections, and active portfolio monitoring rather than reliance on external
credit ratings. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; margin-left:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Qualifying Asset Requirements; <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">Non-U.S.</FONT> Investments </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">As a BDC, at least 70% of the Fund&#8217;s assets must be the type of &#8220;qualifying&#8221; assets listed in Section&nbsp;55(a) of the 1940
Act, which are generally privately offered securities issued by U.S. private or thinly traded companies. The Fund may also invest up to 30% of its portfolio opportunistically in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;non-qualifying&#8221;</FONT>
portfolio investments, such as investments in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-U.S.</FONT> companies. Any <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-U.S.</FONT> investments will be subject to the same underwriting standards and return requirements as
the Fund&#8217;s domestic investments. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; margin-left:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Leverage </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Fund intends to use leverage to seek to enhance investment returns and increase the capital available for investment. In addition to the
Atlas Credit Facility, the Fund expects to incur leverage through one or more senior credit facilities, subscription facilities, or other borrowing arrangements, which may include debt securitization transactions, unsecured notes issuances and/or
financing through special purpose vehicles designed to optimize the Fund&#8217;s cost of capital and investment capacity. As a BDC, the Fund is subject to the asset coverage requirements of the 1940 Act, which generally limit the Fund&#8217;s
ability to incur indebtedness unless it maintains an asset coverage ratio of at least 150% (<I>i.e.</I>, a <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">debt-to-equity</FONT></FONT> ratio of no greater than 2:1), following
satisfaction of the applicable approval requirements under Section&nbsp;61(a) of the 1940 Act. Our initial shareholders approved the adoption of this 150% threshold pursuant to Section&nbsp;61(a)(2) of the 1940 Act on October 1, 2026 and October 27,
2026. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; margin-left:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Hedging </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Fund may enter into hedging transactions to reduce the risk of adverse movements in interest rates, currency exchange rates, or other
market factors that may affect the value of the Fund&#8217;s portfolio or the cost of its liabilities. Hedging instruments may include interest rate swaps, interest rate caps and floors, foreign currency forward contracts, futures contracts, and
other derivative instruments. There can be no assurance that the Fund&#8217;s hedging activities will be effective. The Fund is not required to hedge any particular risk and may choose not to do so. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Potential Market Opportunity </B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We believe
that the financial sponsor-backed private credit market has become increasingly crowded and commoditized, with many established firms allocating significant capital to the space and newer entrants also predominantly focused on sponsor-backed
transactions. As a result, direct lending in the sponsor market has become highly competitive, contributing to yield compression, increased leverage and deterioration in credit terms and documentation. </P>

 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In contrast, the Fund will seek to invest primarily in the
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-sponsor</FONT> middle market, which we believe remains generally underserved. In our experience, opportunities in this segment are more difficult to source and often arise only after meaningful trust has been
developed with a potential issuer. Transactions in the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-sponsor</FONT> middle market frequently require a greater investment of time and resources than private equity-sponsored transactions, which often proceed on

opportunities. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We believe the Fund can generate attractive risk-adjusted returns in the
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-sponsor</FONT> middle market by generally investing in secured loans and adhering to highly structured documentation, including strong covenants and limitations on cash leakage, such as dividends. Whereas
sponsor-backed private credit firms often focus on developing relationships with and servicing sponsors, our primary focus is on developing relationships directly with entrepreneurs and management teams. By maintaining direct relationships with
borrowers, we believe we may be better positioned to monitor investments closely, source <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">follow-on</FONT> transactions and provide additional support to portfolio companies. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We further believe that recent market and economic dislocations have improved the opportunity set in the
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-sponsor</FONT> market. Increasing macroeconomic uncertainty has driven meaningful market dislocations, which we believe are creating compelling opportunities and enhancing the attractiveness of the Fund&#8217;s
disciplined credit strategy. Traditional funding sources have become more cautious and retrenched, which we believe has contributed to more favorable supply and demand dynamics in private credit, including higher credit spread premiums and tighter
covenant structures that we believe benefit lenders. Current market volatility has also opened cross-border investment opportunities. We have observed these changes through an increase in actionable opportunities, including bespoke transactions and
complex syndications. We believe otherwise healthy businesses are seeking additional liquidity to navigate an uncertain macroeconomic environment, while certain forced sellers of credit are seeking liquidity on an expedited basis. Our senior
investment team has experience navigating prior economic disruptions, protecting investor value through periods of dislocation, and identifying advantageous investment environments. Collectively, we believe these dynamics present a potentially
attractive investment opportunity for the Fund. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Potential Competitive Strengths </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Our core business is the disciplined management of risk. We seek to be highly selective in the opportunities we pursue, dedicating the time and
resources necessary to conduct independent diligence, structure appropriate protections and underwrite investments with what we believe to be attractive risk-adjusted return potential. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We focus on the middle market and <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-sponsor</FONT> sectors, where we believe borrowers often have more
complex financing needs than larger companies and may require more flexible capital solutions to support growth, acquisitions, refinancings or other strategic initiatives. We believe there are relatively fewer lenders serving these companies today,
particularly as many private credit platforms have reduced focus on the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-sponsored</FONT> market during the last ten years as their funds have grown. In addition, following the pandemic, we believe traditional
bank lenders have become subject to more regulatory scrutiny, while many <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-bank</FONT> lenders remain focused on sponsor-backed transactions, which they may believe often benefit from faster timelines and
sponsor-prepared diligence materials that can expedite the underwriting process. As a result, we believe many entrepreneur- and management-owned businesses seeking flexible financing solutions are underserved by traditional lenders, creating an
attractive opportunity for experienced <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-sponsor</FONT> lenders. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We believe our sourcing model is
differentiated and well-suited to accessing these opportunities. Our investment team has developed a broad network of relationships across banks, broker-dealers, accountants, lawyers, middle market intermediaries and other referral channels, which
we believe enables us to source bespoke and proprietary transactions. Based on the team&#8217;s prior experience at leading institutions, we believe the team has developed a reputation as a trusted partner with the ability to evaluate and execute
complex transactions. The Adviser&#8217;s origination channels and sourcing infrastructure are described in greater detail under &#8220;<I>Investment Process</I>&#8221; below. </P>

diligence and disciplined transaction structuring. The Fund will often seek to mitigate principal risk by investing in senior secured positions within borrowers&#8217; capital structures and by
selecting companies with what we believe are strong management teams, durable business models, healthy cash flows, conservative capital structures and appropriate structural protections. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Investment Types </B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; margin-left:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Senior Loans
</I></B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Senior loans are debt obligations typically arranged by banks or other financial institutions on behalf of corporations,
partnerships and other business issuers. Proceeds from senior loans may be used for a variety of purposes, including general corporate purposes, refinancings, capital expenditures, leveraged buyouts, mergers and acquisitions and other strategic
initiatives. The Fund&#8217;s senior loans will generally have stated terms of five to seven years, although the expected average life of such instruments is generally between three and four years. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Senior loans are referred to as &#8220;senior&#8221; because they generally occupy a senior position in the borrower&#8217;s capital structure
and are typically secured by a first or second priority lien on the borrower&#8217;s assets. As a result, senior loans generally have priority over junior debt, preferred equity and common equity with respect to payment and recovery in the event of
borrower distress or insolvency. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In connection with the Fund&#8217;s senior loan investments, the Fund generally expects to obtain
security interests in certain assets of the borrower, and consequently such assets are expected to serve as collateral in support of the repayment of such senior loans. This collateral may take the form of first or second priority liens on the
assets of a portfolio company. The collateral supporting senior loans may include a broad range of assets, including working capital assets, such as accounts receivable and inventory; tangible fixed assets, such as real property, buildings and
equipment; intangible assets, such as trademarks, patents and other intellectual property rights; and security interests in the equity interests of the borrower&#8217;s subsidiaries and affiliates. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">If a borrower becomes distressed or enters into bankruptcy proceedings, senior lenders are typically entitled to repayment before payments are
made to bondholders, preferred shareholders or common equity holders. Although there can be no assurance that collateral will be sufficient to repay a senior loan in full, senior loans have historically experienced higher recovery rates than
unsecured or subordinated debt instruments, including high yield bonds. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">&#8220;Floating rate&#8221; refers to loans where the interest
paid changes as certain market interest rates change. Senior loans are typically structured as floating rate instruments that pay interest at a variable rate based on a stated spread over a reference rate, such as the Secured Overnight Financing
Rate (&#8220;<U>SOFR</U>&#8221;). The stated spread is intended to reflect, among other things, the credit risk of the applicable borrower. The reference rate typically resets periodically, often every 30 to 90 days, so that the loan&#8217;s
interest rate adjusts to changes in prevailing market rates. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Senior loans may also include SOFR floors, which establish a minimum
reference rate for purposes of calculating the interest payable on the loan. A SOFR floor can help preserve a minimum level of yield to lenders even when prevailing SOFR rates fall below the agreed-upon floor. In our recent experience, SOFR floors
have become a common feature of new senior loan issuances, and such floors are typically between 0.50% and 2.00%. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Senior loans also
generally include protective covenant packages in favor of the lender or lender group. These covenants are designed to provide lenders with additional downside protection and ongoing visibility into borrower performance. Such covenants may include
affirmative covenants (including financial reporting requirements), negative covenants (including limitations on the incurrence of additional indebtedness, restrictions on asset sales, and restrictions on dividends and other payments), financial
maintenance covenants, lien protection, change of control provisions and board observation or participation rights. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Senior loans may
include both revolving lines of credit and term loans. Senior loans generally have floating interest rates, which may have interest rate floors, and may also provide for some amortization of principal and excess
</P>

<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In addition to senior loans, the Fund expects to invest, to a lesser extent, in asset-based opportunities, such as whole loans, CLOs, private
securitizations or similar privately negotiated instruments, public securitizations, interests in diversified pools of loans or receivables and related equity investments, including funds and/or pooled investment vehicles managed by us or one or
more third-party managers, that have the potential to generate attractive yields with downside protection. The Fund may invest in debt and equity tranches of such instruments at various levels of the capital structure, including, in certain cases,
first-loss or subordinated positions. These investments are generally secured by, or otherwise linked to the performance of, discrete pools of collateral. The Fund believes such asset-based structures can provide additional diversification and
downside protection within the broader portfolio. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">CLOs are structured credit securities backed by a pool of loans, typically <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-investment</FONT> grade, first lien senior secured corporate bank loans. CLOs are structured as multiple tranches that offer investors varying degrees of credit risk, maturity and yield characteristics. CLO tranches
are typically categorized as senior debt, mezzanine debt or subordinated equity according to their relative seniority, payment priority and degree of risk. If the collateral underlying a given CLO defaults or otherwise underperforms, scheduled
payments to senior tranches take precedence over those of more junior tranches. The Fund&#8217;s CLO investments may include senior or mezzanine CLO debt tranches or subordinated CLO equity tranches. CLO equity tranches are generally entitled to
receive residual cash flows from the collateral pool after the debt tranches have received their required interest and principal payments, and accordingly involve a greater degree of risk. The Fund may also invest in warehouse facilities that hold
loans in anticipation of expected CLO issuance. The Fund may invest in asset-based opportunities through direct purchases, through funds and/or pooled investment vehicles managed by us or one or more third-party managers, or through joint ventures
or special purpose vehicles formed for the purpose of acquiring and managing such assets. There can be no assurance that these investments will perform as expected, and the value of the Fund&#8217;s asset-based investments may be affected by, among
other things, changes in interest rates, prepayment rates, default rates and the performance of the underlying collateral pools. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; margin-left:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Healthcare and Royalty Lending </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Fund also expects to invest, to a lesser extent, in healthcare and royalty lending, including credit backed by royalties or other cash flow
streams associated with approved and commercialized biopharmaceutical products, diagnostics and medical devices. Healthcare and royalty lending investments may take the form of royalty purchases, synthetic royalty transactions, asset-backed credit
secured by contractual revenue streams, or structured credit facilities collateralized by royalty or milestone payments. In royalty purchase transactions, the Fund may acquire the right to receive a portion or all of the royalties payable on net
sales of one or more commercialized products in exchange for an upfront cash payment, and such arrangements may include caps on total payments to the Fund and provisions for reversion of the royalty stream to the seller upon achievement of a
specified return. In synthetic royalty transactions, the Fund may provide capital to a borrower in exchange for periodic payments calculated as a percentage of the borrower&#8217;s product revenues, without acquiring the underlying intellectual
property or regulatory approvals. The Fund believes these opportunities can offer </P>

<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">BSLs are typically originated and structured by banks on behalf of large corporate borrowers with employee counts, revenues, EBITDAs and
enterprise values that may be larger than those of the Fund&#8217;s typical middle market borrowers. The proceeds of BSLs are often used for leveraged buyout transactions, mergers and acquisitions, recapitalizations, refinancings and financing
capital expenditures. BSLs are typically distributed by the arranging bank to a diverse group of investors primarily consisting of collateralized loan obligations, senior secured loan and high yield bond mutual funds,
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">closed-end</FONT> funds, hedge funds, banks, insurance companies and finance companies. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">With respect to
BSLs, the Fund&#8217;s investment strategy will focus on maximizing total return through a combination of current yield and price appreciation. We will seek to deliver attractive risk-adjusted returns by applying a fundamental, value-oriented
investment process designed to construct a portfolio with long-term return potential. Individual investment decisions with respect to BSLs will generally be based on the following principles: </P>

the Fund generally expects to serve as the lead lender and to retain primary responsibility for the negotiation of credit documentation, ongoing monitoring and lender communications. Club deal transactions are generally made by a small group of
investment firms and may provide the Fund with the ability to invest in larger transactions than it could on its own, while also providing the borrower with certainty of financing without the syndication risk typically associated with broadly
distributed loan markets. The <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">co-investment</FONT> partners in such transactions may include other funds managed by us or our affiliates, as well as third-party investors, in each case subject to applicable
regulatory requirements, including the requirements of the 1940 Act. </P>

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; margin-left:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Unitranche Loans </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Unitranche loans are loans that combine features of traditional first lien senior secured, second lien and subordinated debt, generally in a
first lien position. A unitranche loan may extend deeper in a borrower&#8217;s capital structure than traditional first lien debt, and in many cases the lender may provide the borrower most, if not all, of the debt capital structure above equity.
The primary advantages to the borrower of a unitranche structure are the ability to negotiate the entire debt financing with one lender and the elimination of intercreditor issues. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Unitranche loans may provide for a waterfall of cash flow priority among different lenders, commonly structured through <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;first-out&#8221;</FONT> and <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;last-out&#8221;</FONT> payment streams. In limited instances, the Fund may retain the
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;last-out&#8221;</FONT> portion of a unitranche loan. <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;Last-out&#8221;</FONT> first lien loans have a secondary priority behind super-senior
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;first-out&#8221;</FONT> first lien loans in the collateral securing the loans in certain circumstances. The arrangements for a <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;last-out&#8221;</FONT> first lien loan are
typically set forth in an &#8220;agreement among lenders,&#8221; which provides lenders with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;first-out&#8221;</FONT> and <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;last-out&#8221;</FONT> payment streams based on
a single lien on the collateral. Since the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;first-out&#8221;</FONT> lenders generally have priority over the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;last-out&#8221;</FONT> lenders for receiving payment under
certain specified events of default, or upon the occurrence of other triggering events under intercreditor agreements or agreements among lenders, the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;last-out&#8221;</FONT> lenders bear a greater risk of loss
and, in exchange, receive a higher effective interest rate, through arrangements among the lenders, than the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;first-out&#8221;</FONT> lenders or lenders in stand-alone first lien loans. Agreements among lenders
also typically provide greater voting rights to the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;last-out&#8221;</FONT> lenders than the intercreditor agreements to which second lien lenders often are subject. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Among the types of first lien debt in which the Fund may invest, <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;last-out&#8221;</FONT> first lien
loans generally have higher effective interest rates than other types of first lien loans, since <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;last-out&#8221;</FONT> first lien loans rank below stand-alone first lien loans. Unitranche structures may
expose the Fund to certain risks associated with second lien and subordinated debt to the extent the Fund invests in the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;last-out&#8221;</FONT> tranche or subordinated portion of the unitranche loan.
Unitranche loans are typically structured as floating rate instruments priced with a stated spread to SOFR. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; margin-left:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Second Lien Loans
</I></B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Second lien loans are secured loans that have a secondary priority behind first lien debt with respect to the collateral securing
the loan. Second lien debt typically is senior on a lien basis to unsecured liabilities in the borrower&#8217;s capital structure and has the benefit of a security interest over assets of the borrower, though ranking junior to first lien debt
secured by those assets. First lien lenders and second lien lenders typically have separate liens on the collateral, and an intercreditor agreement generally provides the first lien lenders with priority over the second lien lenders&#8217; liens on
the collateral. Because of their junior ranking relative to first lien loans, second lien loans generally carry a higher stated interest rate than first lien loans to compensate lenders for the additional credit risk. Second lien loans may also be
referred to as subordinated loans or subordinated notes. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In the event of a borrower&#8217;s default or bankruptcy, second lien lenders
are generally entitled to repayment only after all first lien obligations have been satisfied from the collateral proceeds, but before unsecured creditors and equity holders receive distributions. As a result, second lien loans carry greater risk of
loss than first lien loans. In connection with its second lien investments, the Fund may receive additional yield enhancements such as warrants to buy common or preferred stock or limited liability company interests. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; margin-left:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Unsecured and Subordinated Loans </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Fund may invest, to a lesser extent, in unsecured and subordinated loans. Unsecured loans are debt obligations that are not secured by any
lien on the borrower&#8217;s assets and therefore do not have the benefit of collateral support. Subordinated loans are debt instruments that rank junior in right of payment to other more senior indebtedness of the borrower. Unsecured and
subordinated loans may carry higher stated interest rates than senior secured loans to compensate lenders for the additional credit risk associated with the absence of collateral or the subordinate position in the borrower&#8217;s capital structure.
</P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">26 </P>

</DIV></Center>

<h5 align="left" style="font-size:10pt;font-weight:bold"><a href="#toc">Table of Contents</a></h5>


<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In the event of a borrower&#8217;s default or bankruptcy, holders of unsecured and
subordinated debt are generally entitled to repayment only after all senior secured obligations have been satisfied, and there can be no assurance that sufficient assets will remain to satisfy unsecured or subordinated claims. The lack of a security
interest in borrower assets may adversely affect recovery rates on unsecured and subordinated investments in a distressed or bankruptcy scenario. As a result, these investments involve a greater degree of risk than senior secured investments. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; margin-left:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Mezzanine Loans </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Mezzanine loans are debt investments that structurally rank subordinate in priority of payment to first lien and second lien debt. Mezzanine
debt is often unsecured and may not have the benefit of the financial maintenance covenants common in first lien and second lien debt. However, mezzanine debt ranks senior to common and preferred equity in a borrower&#8217;s capital structure. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Mezzanine debt investments generally offer lenders fixed or floating interest rate returns, which may include a
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;paid-in-kind&#8221;</FONT></FONT> component, and may also provide lenders an opportunity to participate in the capital appreciation, if any, of a borrower through an equity
interest. This equity interest typically takes the form of an equity <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">co-investment,</FONT> warrants, preferred stock or other equity-linked instruments. Due to its higher risk profile and often less restrictive
covenants compared to senior secured loans, mezzanine debt generally bears a higher stated interest rate than first lien and second lien debt. In some cases, the Fund may enter into mezzanine loans that, by their terms, convert into equity or
additional debt or defer payments of interest (or at least cash interest) for an initial period following the Fund&#8217;s investment. The Fund&#8217;s mezzanine debt investments will generally have stated terms of up to ten years, although the
expected average life of such instruments is generally shorter. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; margin-left:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Equity Securities </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Fund&#8217;s investment in a portfolio company could include an equity or equity-linked interest, such as common stock, preferred stock,
warrants, options, profit participation rights or limited liability company interests. In connection with its debt investments, the Fund may receive equity interests as additional consideration. The Fund may also purchase or otherwise acquire
minority interests in the form of common or preferred equity or equity-related securities, such as rights and warrants that may be converted into or exchanged for common stock or other equity interests, generally in conjunction with one of the
Fund&#8217;s debt investments or through a <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">co-investment</FONT> with a financial sponsor. In certain instances, the Fund may make direct equity investments, although these situations are generally expected to be
limited to those cases where the Fund is also making an investment in a more senior part of the borrower&#8217;s capital structure. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The
Fund&#8217;s equity investments are typically not expected to be control-oriented investments, and the Fund may seek to structure such equity investments to include provisions protecting its rights as a minority-interest holder, including board
observation or information rights and anti-dilution protections. Equity investments involve a greater degree of risk than debt investments, as equity holders are last in line with respect to priority of payment behind all creditors in the event of a
borrower&#8217;s distress or insolvency. As a result, the Fund may lose its entire investment in any equity position. To the extent the Fund receives equity or equity-linked consideration in connection with a debt investment, such equity
participation is intended to enhance the Fund&#8217;s total return on the overall investment. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; margin-left:2%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Other Private Credit Opportunities
</I></B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Fund may also pursue other private credit opportunities and additional asset classes from time to time, including <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">co-investments</FONT> with other Sagard credit strategies and relationships with banks, in each case where such opportunities are consistent with the Fund&#8217;s investment objective and its focus on senior secured
lending to U.S. middle market companies as its primary investment strategy. </P>
